los.los_text: Describe the steps in the financial statement analysis framework
los.why_recommended: Schweser lists the six steps clearly. Question banks test step classification heavily (17 questions), and the answer often depends on Curriculum Exhibit 1 (sources and outputs of each phase) — read the 4 Extras, especially the forecasts conflict.
los.why_not_other: Curriculum pp.5–9 repeats the same steps with long narrative; Exhibit 1 is the only part you need and it is summarised in the Extras.
los.sch_anchor: The financial statement analysis framework sets out

los.los_text: Describe the roles of financial statement analysis
los.why_recommended: Same definition and decision examples. The most tested trap — reporting provides information, analysis uses it to make decisions — is fully covered in Schweser.
los.why_not_other: Curriculum adds news examples (Sea Ltd, T-Mobile) — context only.
los.sch_anchor: Financial reporting refers to the way companies
los.curr_anchor: The role of financial statement analysis is to use financial reports

los.los_text: Describe the importance of regulatory filings, financial statement notes and supplementary information, management’s commentary, and audit reports
los.why_recommended: Largest LOS (about half of all questions). Curriculum is more complete on segments, audit assurance, filings and management commentary, and Schweser conflicts with it on 4 points. After reading, check the 4 Schweser-only Extras — question banks test them.
los.why_not_other: Schweser first would duplicate ~75% and still leave gaps; use it as a 10-minute review afterwards.
los.curr_anchor: Regulatory authorities require publicly traded issuers

los.los_text: Describe implications for financial analysis of alternative financial reporting systems and the importance of monitoring developments in financial reporting standards
los.why_recommended: Schweser has the identical IFRS vs US GAAP table; add four Curriculum points (no reconciliation, convergence status, user perspective).
los.why_not_other: Curriculum adds the 2007 CFA position paper and comment-letter process — rarely tested.
los.sch_anchor: While the IASB and FASB work together
los.curr_anchor: The adoption of IFRS as the required financial reporting standard

los.los_text: Describe information sources that analysts use in financial statement analysis besides annual and interim financial reports
los.why_recommended: Same four-way classification and examples in half the length.
los.why_not_other: Curriculum adds consultancy names and the management-bias remark.
los.sch_anchor: As well as regulated information provided by issuers
los.curr_anchor: In addition to regulated information from issuers

extras.title: Exhibit 1: what each phase produces
extras.full_text: Purpose → statement of objective, questions, report content, timetable. Collect → usable financial data, questionnaires. Process → adjusted statements, common-size statements, ratios and graphs. Analyze/interpret → analytical results, forecasts, valuations. Develop & communicate → report answering Phase-1 questions and a recommendation. Follow-up → actual vs expected, revised forecasts, updated reports.
extras.exam_link: Curriculum Q1–2; UWorld Q1,Q4,Q5; AP Q4568,Q4570,Q4572

extras.title: Ratios: output of one step, input to the next
extras.full_text: Ratios are OUTPUTS of "Process data" and INPUTS to "Analyze/interpret". Asked "ratios are an input into which step?" → Analyze/interpret.

extras.title: Forecasts: building vs using (see conflict CF-07)
extras.full_text: The Curriculum lists "making forecasts" and "performing valuations" as processing activities in the text, but Exhibit 1 shows forecasts and valuations as outputs of Analyze/interpret. Rule for questions: PREPARING/BUILDING a forecast model from collected data → Process data; forecasts and valuations used to reach a conclusion → Analyze/interpret.

extras.title: Define the question before computing ratios
extras.full_text: Do not start calculating ratios before knowing which decision the analysis supports; define audience, deliverable, deadline and resources (resource constraints belong to Phase 1). Data collection often follows a top-down approach: economy → industry → company.

extras.title: Report contents and Standard V(B)
extras.full_text: An equity report typically includes: summary and conclusion, industry and competitive analysis, financial model/scenarios, valuation, investment risks. Standard V(B): separate facts from opinions, disclose limitations and risks. An opinion on the fairness of statements is the auditor’s job, not part of the analyst report.

extras.title: Central focus of financial analysis
extras.full_text: Can the company (1) earn a return on capital at least equal to its cost of capital, (2) grow profitably, (3) generate enough cash to meet obligations and pursue opportunities? The role of analysis is to FORM EXPECTATIONS about future performance and position for economic decisions; providing information is the role of financial reporting.

extras.title: Managers vs external analysts
extras.full_text: Managers also analyse the company but do not rely only on financial statements because they have non-public information.

extras.title: Sea Ltd and T-Mobile examples
extras.full_text: Earnings news is judged against analysts’ expectations (equity view); rating actions focus on leverage and free cash flow (credit view).

extras.title: Definition of an operating segment
extras.full_text: A component that (1) may earn revenue and incur expenses (a start-up segment qualifies), (2) has results regularly reviewed by the chief operating decision maker (CODM), and (3) has discrete financial information.

extras.title: Reportable segment thresholds
extras.full_text: Report a segment if it is ≥10% of the COMBINED operating segments’ revenue, assets or |profit| (profit test vs the greater of total profits or total losses). If reportable segments’ external revenue is <75% of TOTAL revenue, add segments until 75%. Others go to "all other segments".

extras.title: Required segment disclosures
extras.full_text: Revenue (external vs inter-segment); profit or loss; assets and liabilities only if reviewed by the CODM; interest revenue/expense; PP&E and intangibles acquired; D&A; other non-cash expenses; income tax; equity-method share. Plus factors used to identify segments and a reconciliation to consolidated totals. Segment COGS / full statements are NOT required.

extras.title: Major customer disclosure
extras.full_text: A customer ≥10% of total revenue must be disclosed (not its identity) — concentration risk.

extras.title: Notes: flexibility reduces comparability
extras.full_text: Notes give basis of preparation and accounting policies, methods and estimates. Choices (e.g., depreciation method, useful life) reflect each firm’s economics but reduce comparability, so analysts adjust. Notes also cover acquisitions/disposals, contractual and off-balance-sheet obligations, financial-instrument risks, legal proceedings, related parties, subsequent events.

extras.title: Reasonable, not absolute, assurance
extras.full_text: Audits use sampling and statements contain estimates → only REASONABLE assurance of fair presentation ("true and fair view"): a high probability of no MATERIAL error, fraud or illegal acts. Never a guarantee; preventing fraud is not the objective.

extras.title: Four audit opinions
extras.full_text: Unqualified (clean) — preferred. Qualified — scope limitation OR exception to standards ("except for..."). Adverse — materially not fairly presented. Disclaimer — unable to issue an opinion.
extras.exam_link: Curriculum Q12–13; UWorld Q11; AP Q5044; CF-02

extras.title: Key vs Critical Audit Matters
extras.full_text: KAM (international, ISA 701): matters the auditor considers most important. CAM (US, PCAOB AS 3101): especially challenging, subjective or complex auditor judgment. NOT necessarily the most important factors for analysts.

extras.title: Interim reports are unaudited
extras.full_text: 10-Q (quarterly, US) and 6-K (semiannual, many non-US) contain unaudited statements and an interim MD&A.

extras.title: Annual report vs Form 10-K
extras.full_text: 10-K / 20-F / 40-F are required annual SEC filings (8-K is a current report, not annual). The polished annual report to shareholders is NOT an SEC requirement.

extras.title: Registration statement contents
extras.full_text: Disclosures about the securities, relation to other securities, annual-filing information, recent audited statements, RISK FACTORS. No projections, no underwriter opinions.

extras.title: Management commentary: five elements
extras.full_text: IFRS Practice Statement (guidance, not a standard): nature of business; objectives and strategies; resources, risks and relationships; results; critical performance measures. US MD&A must cover trends and uncertainties affecting liquidity, capital resources and results; inflation; off-balance-sheet and contractual obligations; critical accounting policies. Mostly unaudited.
extras.exam_link: Curriculum Q11; AP Q344, Q1811, Q5054; CF-08, CF-09

extras.title: US securities laws and SOX
extras.full_text: 1933 Act: registration of new issues. 1934 Act: created the SEC, periodic reporting. SOX 2002: created the PCAOB; restricts non-audit services; executives certify statements; management reports on internal control and the auditor attests.

extras.title: Other SEC forms
extras.full_text: 8-K/6-K current reports; Forms 3/4/5 insider ownership; Form 144 notice of proposed sale of restricted/affiliate securities; 11-K employee plans; DEF-14A proxy. Forms are rarely tested.

extras.title: IOSCO is not a regulator
extras.full_text: IOSCO members regulate >95% of markets but IOSCO itself does not regulate or enforce; it is a platform for common standards. Three objectives: protect investors; fair, efficient, transparent markets; REDUCE (not eliminate) systemic risk.

extras.title: EU endorsement process
extras.full_text: EU listed companies use IFRS since 2005; ESC advises, ESMA coordinates supervision.

extras.title: Sea Ltd segment, MD&A and audit report
extras.full_text: E-commerce >50% of revenue but loss-making; clean opinion with two CAMs.

extras.title: Three parts of the standard auditor’s opinion
extras.full_text: (1) Statements are management’s responsibility; the auditor performed an independent review. (2) Generally accepted auditing standards were followed → reasonable assurance of no material errors. (3) Statements follow accepted accounting principles and the principles and estimates are reasonable. Extra explanation if methods were not applied consistently.
extras.anchor: The standard auditor’s opinion contains three parts
extras.exam_link: Schweser QBank Q9, Q12; AP Q1792

extras.title: Explanatory paragraph for material uncertainty
extras.full_text: Added when a material loss is probable but cannot be estimated — going-concern doubt, asset valuation, litigation. A statement that GAAP was followed is part of the standard report, not an explanatory paragraph.

extras.title: Footnotes are audited; MD&A is not
extras.full_text: Notes are an integral part of the financial statements and are covered by the audit opinion; management commentary is largely unaudited; interim reports and press releases are unaudited.
extras.exam_link: Schweser QBank Q2, Q20; UWorld Q15; AP Q1803

extras.title: IFRS recommends, regulators require
extras.full_text: IFRS guidance RECOMMENDS the content of management commentary; it is not required by accounting standards. Securities regulators (e.g., SEC) may require it.

extras.title: Internal control responsibility
extras.full_text: Internal controls are management’s responsibility (not the board’s). For US public firms the auditor gives an opinion on internal control (separately or as a fourth element of the report). Weak controls allow low-quality or fraudulent reporting.

extras.title: Using segment data
extras.full_text: Segment margins, asset turnover and ROA, and segment growth rates help forecast sales and profits.
extras.anchor: Both US GAAP and IFRS require

extras.title: No reconciliation between IFRS and US GAAP
extras.full_text: Reconciliation disclosures are not required → analysts often lack the data to adjust and must interpret cross-standard comparisons with caution.

extras.title: Status of convergence
extras.full_text: Convergence of frameworks paused in the late 2000s, but major new standards (revenue, leases, credit losses) are mostly converged.
extras.anchor: In general, the IASB and FASB

extras.title: Monitor as a user, not a preparer
extras.full_text: An accountant monitors standards as a preparer; an analyst as a user — how changes affect reports and valuation.

extras.title: New products and window dressing
extras.full_text: New transactions may lack guidance or be designed for window dressing. Be suspicious when management cannot explain the business purpose.
extras.anchor: New Products or Types of Transactions

extras.title: Exposure drafts; recognition vs disclosure
extras.full_text: Analysts can read exposure drafts and submit comment letters. Items recognized in statements get more rigor than items only disclosed in notes.

extras.title: 2007 CFA Institute position paper
extras.full_text: Fair value, neutrality, direct-method cash flow statement.

extras.title: Bias in issuer communications
extras.full_text: Earnings calls are not legally required; management is biased → ask probing questions. Issuer communications are unaudited and not objective (press releases).

extras.title: Internal vs external sources
extras.full_text: External = not produced by the company (peer analysis, industry and government data, trade publications). Proxy statements, earnings calls and MD&A are company (internal) sources.
extras.anchor: Information on the economy, industry, and peer companies
extras.exam_link: Curriculum Q16; UWorld Q17; AP Q352

extras.title: Industry data providers
extras.full_text: Rystad (energy), IQVIA and Evaluate (biopharma), Gartner and IDC (technology).
